questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why blue light opens stomata faster than red light
questions.stem: An analyst's dashboard note records that blue light opens stomata faster than red light at the same photon flux. What explains the difference?

options.text: Blue light activates phototropins in guard cells, switching on the proton pump and speeding opening
Red light provides more usable energy per photon, so it opens the pores more quickly
options.misconception: treats light quality as a matter of energy per photon alone

options.text: Blue light is absorbed by chlorophyll in the mesophyll, so the pore opens more quickly
options.misconception: credits mesophyll photosynthesis rather than guard receptors

options.text: Red light changes the osmotic potential of the sap, which pulls the guard cells open
options.misconception: invents a bulk osmotic effect of red light on the sap

questions.explanation: Blue light receptors in the guard cell membrane switch on the proton pump, so potassium and water follow and the pore opens. Red light works mainly through photosynthesis and internal carbon dioxide.
questions.hint: Look for the blue light receptor in the guard cell itself.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a phytochrome interconversion experiment
questions.stem: The dashboard shows a phytochrome assay in which red light treatment raised the Pfr fraction of the pigment from 10% to 80%, and far-red light treatment lowered it to 20%. What does this pattern show?

options.text: Red light destroys the pigment while far-red light rebuilds it from scratch
options.misconception: treats the pigment as broken down, not interconverted

options.text: Red light converts Pr to the active Pfr form and far-red light reverses it
Far-red light drives the conversion to the active form and red light blocks it
options.misconception: reverses which colour drives the active form

options.text: Both wavelengths work equally well and the differences are experimental noise
options.misconception: dismisses a repeatable change between treatments as noise

questions.explanation: The pigment switches between two interconvertible forms, with red light converting Pr into Pfr and far-red reversing it. The shifts in Pfr reflect photoconversion, not damage.
questions.hint: Phytochrome exists in two forms that are converted by light.

options.misconception: reads the axis direction as the definition of the plant type

options.text: Both are short-day plants, because any dependence on the night implies a short-day response
options.misconception: assumes any dependence on darkness means short-day behaviour

options.text: X is a short-day plant and Y is a long-day plant, each keyed to a critical day length
Neither can be classified, since flowering here depends only on temperature
options.misconception: denies that day length can classify a photoperiodic response

questions.stem: A note on the dashboard says: winter wheat is sown in autumn because the cold winter provides the long days it needs to flower in spring. Diagnose the error.

options.misconception: conflates the cold requirement with the photoperiodic one

options.misconception: invents a metabolic explanation for vernalisation

options.text: The cold provides the vernalisation requirement, and the long days then trigger flowering

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Photoperiod and flowering in a data set
questions.learningObjective: Design a method to determine a critical day length
questions.stem: Design a way, in dashboard terms, to determine the critical day length for a batch of young plants and to confirm the result.

answer.exemplar: Grow otherwise identical groups of the same age under a series of photoperiods from 8 to 18 hours, keeping temperature, humidity and light intensity the same. Record which groups produce visible flower buds and plot days to flowering against day length. The critical day length is the value at which flowering switches from absent to present, confirmed by repeating the two photoperiods either side of it.

questions.explanation: A critical photoperiod can only be found by bracketing it, so a graded series of day lengths under constant conditions is needed. Confirming it means repeating the photoperiods beside it.
questions.hint: Use a graded series of day lengths, other things constant.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a shoot bends towards unilateral light
questions.stem: Explain, in dashboard language, how a seedling bends towards a light placed to one side of it.

answer.exemplar: Blue light receptors called phototropins in the shoot tip detect the light gradient and trigger lateral transport of auxin away from the lit side. Auxin then accumulates on the shaded side, where it promotes cell elongation, so those cells grow longer than the lit cells and the shoot bends towards the light with its tip pointing at the source.

questions.explanation: The bending follows from a redistribution of auxin rather than from any loss of tissue on the lit side. Because auxin promotes elongation in shoots, the side with more of it grows faster.
questions.hint: Auxin promotes elongation, so ask which side receives more.

questions.explanation: Multiplying the upper side concentration of 40 nanomoles per litre by 1.5 gives 60 nanomoles per litre on the lower side. That gradient is the signal that bends the organ.
questions.hint: Multiply the upper side value by the stated ratio.

questions.stem: The dashboard diagram shows a shoot with the tip removed and two lateral buds below the cut, which then grow out. What principle does that diagram illustrate?

options.misconception: explains bud release by stem length, not by hormones

options.text: Removing the tip supplies extra carbohydrate to the lateral buds below the cut
options.misconception: explains bud release as a purely nutritional effect

options.text: The apical bud suppresses lateral bud growth through auxin, so removing the tip releases them

questions.learningObjective: Order the events linking blue light to stomatal opening
questions.stem: Stage one: the dashboard shows a guard cell assay in which blue light raises the proton pump activity of the plasma membrane. Stage two: the analyst asks what chain of events follows and how the pore responds.

options.text: Pump export hyperpolarises the membrane, potassium enters, water follows and the pore opens
Pump export depolarises the membrane, potassium leaves, water follows and turgor rises
options.misconception: reverses both the electrical response and the ion movement

options.text: Pump export brings protons in, so the cell acidifies, turgor falls and the pore closes
options.misconception: confuses the blue light response with abscisic acid closure

options.text: The pump drives water straight out of the cell, so turgor falls and the pore closes
options.misconception: treats the proton pump as a water pump

questions.explanation: Exporting protons makes the guard cell membrane more negative, which opens potassium channels, so potassium and then water enter and the pore opens. The other options reverse the electrical response.
questions.hint: Proton export makes the membrane more negative, not less.

questions.learningObjective: Design a test of auxin redistribution in gravity response
questions.stem: Design a test, using the dashboard as the record, for whether gravity driven bending of a shoot is driven by auxin redistribution rather than by a change in water content.

answer.exemplar: Place seedlings horizontally with the shoot tip removed and the stump tilted so that an agar block containing auxin is set asymmetrically on one side, with a plain agar block as the control. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the shoot tip maintains apical dominance
questions.stem: For the dashboard, explain how the shoot tip maintains apical dominance over the lateral buds below it.

answer.exemplar: Auxin made in the shoot tip is transported down the stem and suppresses the growth of lateral buds, so the main shoot keeps the plant's resources and the tip stays dominant. Removing the tip removes that source, the inhibition lifts and the lateral buds begin to grow, which is why pruning the tip of a hedge makes it bushier and wider.

questions.explanation: Apical dominance depends on the tip remaining present, so removing or pinching the tip reverses it. The hormone inhibits the lateral buds rather than feeding them.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the buds when the source is removed.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why blue light is used as a night break
questions.stem: For the dashboard, explain why blue light is used as a night break in some glasshouses even though red light drives photosynthesis well.

answer.exemplar: The night break is aimed at the phytochrome system, which governs the length of the night that short-day crops perceive. A brief flash of red light, followed by far-red to undo the response, resets the night and prevents flowering in short-day plants such as chrysanthemums, which lets the grower hold the crop for a planned market date rather than losing control of flowering.

questions.explanation: A night break aims to interrupt the dark period the timing system measures, not to add photosynthate. A red flash with a far-red follow-up resets the clock and then cancels the response.
questions.hint: A night break interrupts darkness rather than adding light.

answer.exemplar: Take matched shoots. questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a shoot tip detects the direction of light
questions.stem: For the analyst, explain how a shoot tip can sense which side of the stem the light is on.

answer.exemplar: The tip contains phototropins, blue light receptors that are activated more strongly on the lit side of the organ. That asymmetry switches on lateral auxin transport in the tip so that auxin moves to the shaded side, and the resulting difference in cell elongation bends the shoot towards the light. A level tip receives equal light on both sides, so it stays straight.

questions.explanation: Sensing depends on an asymmetric distribution of receptor activation across the tip, not on simply detecting light. The graded response then drives lateral auxin transport.
questions.hint: The receptor is activated more on one side than the other.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why vernalisation is a requirement rather than a growth effect
questions.stem: The analyst asks why vernalisation is described as a cold requirement rather than a low temperature effect on growth. Explain for the dashboard.

answer.exemplar: Vernalisation is the sustained exposure of a germinating seed or young plant to a period of low temperature that leaves it able to flower. The effect persists for months after the cold ends, so it is a change in the competence of the plant rather than a slow-down of growth. It is also distinct from photoperiodism, which still decides when the flower actually opens.

questions.explanation: The lasting nature of the effect separates vernalisation from a change in growth rate, since a chilled plant behaves differently long after it warms. It is separate from photoperiodism.
questions.hint: Ask whether the effect outlasts the cold treatment.

answer.exemplar: Grow groups of cuttings under photoperiods of 8, 10, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 16 hours, with identical temperature, humidity and light intensity, and record the date the first flower bud appears. questions.stem: For the analyst, explain why the ratio of red to far-red light is used as an index of shading in crop canopies.

answer.exemplar: Red light is absorbed strongly by chlorophyll, so a canopy rich in leaves absorbs red but transmits and reflects much more of the far-red light. questions.explanation: The ratio reports canopy closure better than total light, because leaves treat the two wavelengths differently. The plant reads that ratio through phytochrome and adjusts its growth.
